attributes.body:
The verb 呉（く）れる in Japanese, is very similar to 与（あた）える (to bestow). The primary difference is that 呉（く）れる (primarily written in hiragana) means to 'bestow to the speaker' (or someone in the speakers inner circle).

In this way, てくれる is the opposite of てあげる, which conveys that someone (usually the speaker) gives (an action) to another person that is outside of their inner circle. てくれる is commonly translated as 'would you do (A) for me', as a question, or 'someone did (A) for me', as a statement.

When asking for a favor, てくれる can be shortened to てくれ. However, this is very casual, and should not be used with strangers (or anyone that you do not know well). As an English equivalent, てくれ sounds similar to phrases like 'would ya do (A)', or 'could ya do (A)?'

Fun Fact

てくれる is one of the most casual ways to ask for a favor, with てもらう being slightly more polite. ていただく (the humble speech variation of てくれる) is even more polite than either of these!

attributes.source: [DBJG] A Dictionary of Basic Japanese Grammar

attributes.description: てあげる vs てくれる vs てもらう
Asking favors with 「くれる」 or 「もらえる」

attributes.body: くれる means 'to give' and is used when someone outside the speaker's group gives something to the speaker or their in-group. For example, プレゼントをくれた means '(someone) gave me a present.' As てくれる, it shows someone did something for the speaker's benefit, as in 日本語を教えてくれた ('(someone) taught me Japanese').

second_relatable.title: てくれる
second_relatable.meaning: To do something for someone (usually you)

attributes.body: Both express receiving a favor, but from different perspectives. With てくれる, the subject is the giver and they do something for you. With てもらう, the subject is the receiver and they get someone to do something. For example, ケンが教えてくれた frames the action as 'Ken taught/told me.', while ケンに教えてもらった frames it as 'I had Ken teach/tell me.'.

first_relatable.title: てくれる
first_relatable.meaning: To do something for someone (usually you)

second_relatable.title: てもらう
second_relatable.meaning: To get someone to do, To have someone do

attributes.body: てくれる describes someone doing something that benefits you, like 来てくれた ('He/you/they came for me.'), implying that their coming helped you. てくれてありがとう specifically expresses gratitude for the action, e.g. 来てくれてありがとう ('Thank you for coming.'). The base meaning is the same, but one contains an explicit message of thanks.

second_relatable.title: てくれる
second_relatable.meaning: To do something for someone (usually you)

attributes.body: Both use the て form with a giving verb to describe doing a favor. てあげる is used when you or someone close to you does something for someone else, e.g. 友達に日本語を教えてあげた ('I taught my friend Japanese.'). In contrast, てくれる is used when someone else does something for you or someone close to you, e.g. 友達が日本語を教えてくれた ('My friend taught me Japanese.').

second_relatable.title: てくれる
second_relatable.meaning: To do something for someone (usually you)

attributes.body: てください is a basic way to express a polite request (e.g., 'Please do...') For example, 食べてください would mean 'Please eat (this).' It is polite and neutral, and can be used with strangers or people equal in status to you. In comparison, てくれる (when used with rising question intonation), is a casual, gentle way of making a request to a close friend or family member.

second_relatable.title: てくれる
second_relatable.meaning: To do something for someone (usually you)

attributes.body: ないでください is used to ask someone not to do something in a polite way. It's relatively neutral and can be used with strangers or people of equal status. In contrast, てくれる, when said with a rising question intonation, is a casual and gentle way to ask a favor from someone close, such as a friend or family member. It feels softer and more familiar than standard polite forms.

second_relatable.title: てくれる
second_relatable.meaning: To do something for someone (usually you)

attributes.body: てくれる shows someone did something for your benefit, like 教えてくれた ('They taught/told me.'). ていただけませんか is a humble and polite way to make a request, e.g. 教えていただけませんか？ ('Would you kindly teach/tell me?'). Both involve benefits for the speaker but differ in tone and usage.
